analysis.one_liner: Bans logging, mining, and road building in the Tongass National Forest and designates roadless areas as wilderness.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: introduced with no cosponsors in October 2000, it was referred to the House Resources Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred new logging, mining, and road construction in Alaska's Tongass National Forest, the largest temperate rain forest in the United States, while honoring contracts already in force. It also would have made every inventoried roadless area in the forest part of the National Wilderness Preservation System, protecting old-growth habitat for bears, eagles, wolves, and salmon. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, members of the public who use or value public lands would gain permanently protected old-growth rain forest, intact wildlife habitat, and undisturbed salmon streams. Alaska's recreation and tourism economy, and the taxpayers who currently fund Forest Service road-building in the Tongass, would also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits activities that disturb or destroy the habitat of indigenous animal and plant species in the Tongass, including road construction, mining, and logging, except under contracts already in force.
It designates all inventoried roadless areas in the Tongass as wilderness under the Wilderness Act, placing them in the National Wilderness Preservation System.
The bill's stated rationale is that subsidizing destruction of pristine temperate rain forest undermines U.S. leadership in urging other countries to protect rain forests.

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry that logs the Tongass, mining companies holding or seeking claims there, and the road construction contractors who build Forest Service logging roads would lose access and future work. Southeast Alaska communities that depend on timber jobs would bear the local economic cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tongass loggers, miners, and road contractors

drawbacks.text: The bill would end logging, mining, and road building in the Tongass with no transition, affecting workers and communities in southeast Alaska whose economies are tied to those activities.
Existing contracts and leases remain in force, so logging and extraction already under contract would continue even while new activity is banned, limiting the bill's immediate effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would permanently protect the nation's largest temperate rain forest at the cost of logging and mining activity in the region. Its grandfathering of existing contracts eases the transition but leaves current extraction untouched. With no committee action, hearing, or vote, its practical effect was zero; its value lies mostly as a statement of what its sponsor wanted protected.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in October 2000 with no cosponsors and referred to the House Resources Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Filner introduced the Tongass Rain Forest Protection Act on October 6, 2000, near the end of the 106th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Resources on the day it was introduced and received no further action.
The bill died at the end of the Congress without a committee hearing or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber and mining interests that operate in the Tongass, along with the communities dependent on that work, are better off because the bill died; nothing in the forest's management changed.

for.name: Rep. Bob Filner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Tongass Rain Forest Protection Act on October 6, 2000.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no member cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of support and opposition never took form in the record.

industries.note: The bill would ban logging in the Tongass, ending access to old-growth timber that the industry now harvests with road subsidies from the Forest Service. Its loss would be the rain forest's gain.
New mineral extraction in the Tongass would be prohibited, though claims and contracts already in force would be honored.
New road construction, largely built to serve logging, would be banned, eliminating future Forest Service road contracts in the forest.
Wilderness designation and intact old-growth habitat protect the scenery and wildlife that draw visitors to southeast Alaska.
